You are interpreting extracted evidence about a lab-device driver.

Task:
- Infer a concise device name (Chinese) and name_en (English).
- Infer the manufacturer from driver evidence (class name, module path,
  docstrings, comments). If unclear, output empty string.
- Write a concise Chinese description and English description_en of the
  physical device and its lab use. Describe the physical device, not the
  software wrapper, backend, API, or driver implementation.
- Write bilingual descriptions for each action.
- For `actions[].action_name`, use the required action id exactly when one is
  provided in the user message under "Required output action ids".
- Some functions are annotated as status_getter or status_setter. These manage
  device properties. For these, the description should simply be
  "get/set/define <plain-text description of the property>".
- Produce tag_hints: a relevance-sorted list of short keyword phrases the
  device relates to (e.g., "cryogenic cooling", "PID temperature control").
  These will be used downstream for tag assignment. Aim for 3-8 hints.
  Prefer English for tag_hints, but Chinese is acceptable if needed.
- Do not invent capabilities unsupported by the evidence.
- If evidence is weak, stay generic rather than hallucinating.
- `name` and `description` must be natural Chinese.
- `name_en` and `description_en` must be natural English.
- Do not copy English text into the Chinese fields.
- Do not describe the result as a "backend", "driver", or "wrapper" unless the
  evidence truly supports only a software component and no physical device can
  be identified.
- Use module path, class name, action surface, and method comments to infer the
  device family when possible.
- Output JSON only.

  Docstring: This is the basic implementation of our FeatureIdentificationDevice (FID)
spectrometer USB API as defined in ENG-0001.
This class is roughly comparable to Wasatch.NET's Spectrometer.cs.

This class is normally not accessed directly, but through the higher-level
abstraction WasatchDevice.

@see ENG-0001
##########################################################################
This class adopts the external device interface structure
This invlovles receiving a request through the handle_request function
A request is processed based on the key in the request
The processing function passes the commands to the requested device
Once it recevies a response from the connected device it then passes that
back up the chain
@verbatim
                           Enlighten Request
                                   |
                            handle_requests
                                   |
                              -----------
                             |  |  |  |  | 
         { get_laser status, acquire, set_laser_watchdog, etc....}
                             |  |  |  |  | 
                              -----------
                                   |
                               _send_code
@endverbatim

  [status_getter] get_laser_temperature_degC(self, raw=None)
    comment: 
    comment: Laser temperature conversion doesn't use EEPROM coeffs at all.
    comment: 
    comment: @par IPS
    comment: 
    comment: Some Wasatch SML products use an IPS Wavelength-Stabilized TO-56
    comment: laser, which internally uses a Betatherm 10K3CG3 thermistor.
    comment: 
    comment: @see https://www.ipslasers.com/data-sheets/SM-TO-56-Data-Sheet-IPS.pdf
    comment: 
    comment: The official IPS conversion from thermistor resistance (in ohms) to degC is:
    comment: 
    comment: \verbatim
    comment: 1 / (   C1
    comment: + C2 * ln(ohms)
    comment: + C3 * pow(ln(ohms), 3)
    comment: )
    comment: - 273.15
    comment: 
    comment: Where: C1 = 0.00113
    comment: C2 = 0.000234
    comment: C3 = 8.78e-8
    comment: \endverbatim
    comment: 
    comment: That said, on XS the IPS thermistor then goes through a MAX1978ETM-T
    comment: TEC IC which buffers the thermistor voltage. This requires the additional
    comment: empirically-determined static conversion captured below.
    comment: 
    comment: Regrettably, the laser thermistor voltage on 110280 boards
    comment: overflows the ADC range, so we don't currently have valid laser
    comment: temperature read-out with those PCBs.
    comment: 
    comment: @par Ondax MML
    comment: 
    comment: On MML units using the Ondax OEM Module, the cable to the 220060
    comment: does not seem to pass-through the thermistor pin, so we don't have
    comment: laser temperature read-out on those, either. (Nor photodiode...)
    comment: 
    comment: @par RealLight
    comment: 
    comment: RealLight SML thermistors use the following resistance and beta:
    comment: 
    comment: Thermistor Rt (kΩ / β(25°C)): 10±5% / 3450
    comment: 
    comment: Therefore you can convert the raw thermistor ADC reading to degrees Celsius:
    comment: 
    comment: 1. Convert raw ADC to voltage:
    comment: 
    comment: voltage = 2.5 * raw / 4096
    comment: 
    comment: 2. Convert voltage to resistance (assuming 2.5v reference)
    comment: 
    comment: resistance = 21450.0 * voltage / (2.5 - voltage)
    comment: 
    comment: 3. Convert resistance to Kelvin:
    comment: 
    comment: 1/T = (1/T0) + (1/β) * ln(R/R0)
    comment: 1 = T((1/T0) + (1/β) * ln(R/10))
    comment: T = 1/((1/T0) + (1/β) * ln(R/10))
    comment: 
    comment: Where:
    comment: 
    comment: T:  is the temperature in Kelvin
    comment: T0: is a reference temperature (usually 25°C or 298.15K)
    comment: β:  is the beta value of the thermistor (a constant indicating the relationship between resistance and temperature)
    comment: R:  is the measured resistance of the thermistor
    comment: R0: is the resistance of the thermistor at the reference temperature T0
    comment: 
    comment: Kelvin = 1/((1/298.15) + (1/3450) * ln(resistance/10))
    comment: 
    comment: 4. Convert Kelvin to degrees Celsius:
    comment: 
    comment: degC = Kelvin - 273.15
    comment: 
    comment: @param raw    the value read from the thermistor's 12-bit ADC (can be
    comment: uint12 or SpectrometerResponse)
    comment: log.debug(msg)
    comment: conversion for 220250 Rev4 MAX1978ETM-T 3V3 buffer -> 12-bit DAC -> degC
    comment: log.debug(f"get_laser_temperature_degC: degC {degC:g} after adding {coeff} x (pow({raw}, {i}) = {pow(raw, i):g})")
    comment: when not using TEC IC

  [command] set_laser_power_high_resolution(self, flag)
    comment: 
    comment: @brief Sets whether the PWM pulse period is 1000µs (high-resolution, default)
    comment: or 100µs (low-resolution, legacy).
    comment: 
    comment: @param flag (Input) True for 1000µs PWM period (high-resolution, default),
    comment: False for 100µs (low-resolution)
    comment: 
    comment: Laser power is controlled via PWM (Pulse Width Modulation), essentially
    comment: a square wave whose "duty cycle" (high vs low), expressed as a percentage,
    comment: represents the amount of time the laser is actually firing. If the duty
    comment: cycle is 33%, the laser will be firing 1/3 of the time, representing
    comment: approximately one-third of "full power".
    comment: 
    comment: (It's not "exactly" one-third because the laser needs a moment to
    comment: stablize when energized, and that "start-up" instability is increased
    comment: when you're constantly pulsing the laser on-and-off.)
    comment: 
    comment: This function is used to determine the LENGTH (period) of that PWM
    comment: square wave.  Because the laser's PWM parameters are all specified in
    comment: microseconds (µs), a longer period allows greater precision (resolution)
    comment: in specifying the duty cycle.
    comment: 
    comment: Historically, Wasatch spectrometers used a PWM period of 100µs, meaning
    comment: the pulse width (time each wave was high) could only be set from 1-99µs,
    comment: giving an essential laser power resolution of 1%.  That behavior can
    comment: be restored by setting this value False.
    comment: 
    comment: More recently, we've increased the default PWM pulse period to 1000µs
    comment: (1ms). Since the pulse width is still set in µs, that allows an
    comment: effective laser power resolution of 0.1%.  This is the new default,
    comment: and can be explicitly requested by setting this value to True.
    comment: 
    comment: @warning Note that this function is provided for cases where the laser power
    comment: is set as a percentage.  When setting laser power through milliWatts, using
    comment: the onboard laser power calibration, it is important to use the same
    comment: resolution as was in effect when the calibration was generated.  All Wasatch
    comment: laser power calibrations are generated in "high-resolution," so this
    comment: function SHOULD NOT be set "False" (low-res) if setting laser power in mW.

  [command] set_laser_power_perc_immediate(self, value)
    comment: 
    comment: Sets laser power (modulated pulse width) which will be used next time the
    comment: laser is turned on (or changed immediately, if the laser is already enabled).
    comment: Laser power is determined by a combination of the pulse width,
    comment: period and modulation being enabled. There are many combinations of
    comment: these values that will produce a given percentage of the total laser
    comment: power through pulse width modulation. There is no 'get laser power'
    comment: control message on the device.
    comment: 
    comment: Some of the goals of Enlighten are for it to be stable, and a reason
    comment: we have sales. During spectrometer builds, it was discovered that
    comment: the laser power settings were not implemented. During the
    comment: implementation process, it was discovered that the laser modulation,
    comment: pulse period and pulse width commands do not conform to
    comment: specification. Where you can set integration time 100 ms with the
    comment: command:
    comment: 
    comment: device.ctrl_transfer(bmRequestType=device_to_host,
    comment: bRequest=0xDB,
    comment: wValue=100,
    comment: wIndex=0,
    comment: data_or_wLength=0)
    comment: 
    comment: The laser pulse period must be set where the wValue and
    comment: data_or_wLength parameters are equal. So if you wanted a pulse
    comment: period of 100, you must specify the value in both places:
    comment: 
    comment: ...
    comment: wValue=100,
    comment: data_or_wLength=100)
    comment: ...
    comment: 
    comment: This in turn implies that the legacy firmware has a long masked
    comment: issue when reading the value to update from the data_or_wLength
    comment: parameter instead of the wValue field. This is only accurate for the
    comment: laser modulation related functions.
    comment: 
    comment: This is backed up by the Dash v3 StrokerControl DLL implementation.
    comment: It was discovered that the StrokerControl DLL sets the wValue and
    comment: data or wLength parameters to the same value at every control
    comment: message write.
    comment: 
    comment: The exciting takeaway here is that Enlighten is stable enough.
    comment: Turning the laser on with the data or wLength parameter not set
    comment: correctly will cause a hardware failure and complete device lockup
    comment: requiring a power cycle.
    comment: 
    comment: fid:
    comment: CRITICAL Hardware Failure FID Send Code Problem with
    comment: ctrl transfer: [Errno None] 11
    comment: 
    comment: Unlike Dash which may lockup and require killing the application,
    comment: Enlighten does not lock up. The Enlighten code base has now been
    comment: used to unmask an issue that has been lurking with our legacy
    comment: firmware for close to 6 years. We've detected this out of
    comment: specification area of the code before it can adversely impact a
    comment: customer. """
    comment: 
    comment: As long as laser power is modulated using a period of 100us,
    comment: with a necessarily-integral pulse width of 1-99us, then it's
    comment: not physically possible to support fractional power levels.
    comment: 
    comment: @todo talk to Jason about changing modulation PERIOD to longer
    comment: value (200us? 400? 1000?), OR whether pulse WIDTH can be
    comment: in smaller unit (500ns? 100ns?)
    comment: If full power (and allowed), disable modulation and exit
    comment: pulse width can't be longer than period, or shorter than 1us
    comment: Change the pulse period.  Note that we're not parsing into 40-bit
    comment: because this implementation is hard-coded to either 100 or 1000us
    comment: (both fitting well within uint16)
    comment: if result.data is None:
    comment: log.critical("Hardware Failure to send laser mod. pulse period")
    comment: return SpectrometerResponse(data=False, error_msg="failed to send laser mod")

    comment: log.critical("Hardware Failure to send pulse width")
    comment: return SpectrometerResponse(data=False, error_msg="failed to send pulse width")
    comment: Enable modulation

    comment: return SpectrometerResponse(data=False, error_msg="failed to send laser modulation")
